μ\mu-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion
in Shared Interaction Voice Agents

Qihao Lin Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Shanghai, China    Guanxu Chen Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Shanghai, China    Shuhang Zheng Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China    Xiaoya Lu Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Shanghai, China    Jingyi Yang Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Shanghai, China Affiliation: Fudan University, Shanghai, China    Terumi Chiba Affiliation: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China    Wenyi Yu Affiliation: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China    Chao Zhang Affiliation: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China    Zhuan Shi Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Shanghai, China Correspondence to: shizhuan@pjlab.org.cn    Jing Shao Affiliation: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Shanghai, China Correspondence to: shaojing@pjlab.org.cn
Abstract

Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce μ\mu-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent’s speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24% tool-free and 65.44% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20%. ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models lag primarily in multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that larger groups consistently degrade joint task success across capable systems. By coupling reactive multi-user simulation with verifiable session-level outcomes, μ\mu-Bench provides a rigorous testbed for shared voice agents.

1 Introduction

Voice agents in shared spaces must serve multiple users whose goals and constraints are often interdependent. Over a single full-duplex audio channel, participants routinely interrupt the agent or speak over one another. Consider a family traveling to the airport: a parent needs to arrive before 10:00, while a child interrupts to request a park detour amid ongoing chatter (Figure 1). Assessing that detour requires checking whether the new route meets the deadline and obtaining the parent’s approval. The agent must track who requested what, identify binding constraints, and reconcile competing goals within each participant’s authority.

In such settings, managing the interaction becomes inseparable from solving the task. A clarification can reveal an unstated constraint, a refusal can prompt an authorized participant to intervene, and an intermediate tool result can change which plans remain feasible. Because subsequent user turns depend directly on the agent’s speech and actions, evaluation must capture this live feedback and score the session as a whole. Depending on the context, the appropriate response may be to fulfill a request, ask for clarification, refuse an unauthorized action, or ignore peer-directed side-talk. Crucially, each such action must remain consistent with all other goals and constraints in the session.

Existing benchmarks address important parts of this problem (Table 1). τ\tau-Voice and Joi-Bench-Task pair interactive voice simulation with verifiable tool execution, covering mid-task revisions, clarifications, and post-interruption recovery, but center on a single simulated user without independent multi-user goals or cross-user permissions (Ray et al., 2026; He et al., 2026). Similarly, DuplexLedger tests transactional memory updates over pre-authored dialogues with adaptive interruption timing and bystander speech (Li et al., 2026). In multi-party settings, MP-Bench, Duplex-MPE, and MultiPartyTurnBench focus on turn-taking, selective participation, and distinguishing barge-ins from backchannels (Shih et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026; Mathur and Manocha, 2026), whereas MultiTalkBench evaluates long-horizon state tracking and participation in recorded group conversations (Wang et al., 2026b). Closer to multi-user task constraints, MSI-Bench examines speaker-scoped memory, disclosure and authority rules, and one-shot tool-call prediction on prerecorded multi-party scenes (Xiong et al., 2026). What remains underexplored is whether an agent can guide multiple participants with interdependent requests to a jointly valid outcome when its own questions, refusals, and tool actions shape what users say and decide next.

To address this gap, we introduce μ\mu-Bench to evaluate multi-user task completion through closed-loop voice interaction. Each scenario specifies participant profiles, goals, permissions, and interaction events. During a session, simulated participants generate contextual responses from their private information and the public dialogue they have heard. An orchestrator schedules events and bounded follow-up exchanges as the conversation evolves. The benchmark spans 100 base scenarios across 20 everyday and professional domains, split between 51 tool-augmented and 49 tool-free scenarios. Tool-augmented tasks test whether agents uphold multi-user constraints during live backend execution, while the shared tool-free track isolates spoken coordination and enables direct comparison with speech models that lack tool-calling support. Varying three binary condition axes (group size, acoustic realism, and follow-up demands) expands these scenarios into 800 evaluation cases and enables matched within-scenario comparisons.

Our primary metric is Joint Task Success (JTS): all required user goals, privacy boundaries, and outcome-level constraints must hold jointly within the same trajectory. Scoring combines programmatic checks on states and tool logs with semantic judgments of recorded responses. Fulfilling one participant’s request cannot compensate for a privacy breach, a missed refusal, or an unresolved requirement elsewhere in the session. In tool-augmented tasks, we further audit unauthorized or misattributed tool executions separately and combine them with JTS into Pure JTS (Section 5.3), exposing agents that reach valid end states through unauthorized execution paths. To diagnose failure modes, we report three complementary diagnostics (ATC): Attribution (addressee routing, participant-role grounding, and request ownership in spoken responses), Threading (maintaining, updating, and resuming user-specific and shared tasks), and Coordination (authorization and privacy compliance alongside service equity).

We evaluate 13 proprietary and open-weight voice agents and find wide capability gaps across both tracks: leading proprietary systems peak at 62.24% Joint Task Success on the tool-free track and 65.44% on tool-augmented tasks, while open-weight models remain below 20% (led by MiniCPM-o 4.5 at 19.39%). ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models combine high boundary compliance with weak multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that increasing group size consistently degrades Joint Task Success across capable systems. A cumulative assistance study on MiniCPM-o 4.5 further shows that serializing overlapping speech and supplying turn-level identity and semantic cues raises Joint Task Success by 61.84% relative, yet still leaves 68.62% of sessions unresolved and points to multi-party planning bottlenecks beyond acoustic concurrency. Our contributions are:

  • •

    A closed-loop task formulation and reactive multi-user simulator that links private participant goals, knowledge, and permissions to live spoken interaction.

  • •

    A suite of 800 controlled cases across 20 domains, combining joint session-level success criteria with Attribution, Threading, and Coordination diagnostics.

  • •

    An empirical evaluation of 13 proprietary and open-weight voice agents via dual-track comparisons, condition contrasts, and cumulative assistance, characterizing failures across concurrent and assisted settings.

2 Related Work

Full-duplex voice agents and single-user task evaluation.

Full-duplex speech models listen and speak simultaneously, supporting natural interruptions, backchannels, and overlapping speech across commercial systems (GPT-Realtime-2, Gemini 3.8 Live, Grok Voice 3.0, MOSS-Live, Seeduplex 3.0 (OpenAI, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026a; Google, 2026; xAI, 2026; OpenMOSS Team, 2026; ByteDance Seed Team, 2026)) and open-weight models (Moshi, Freeze-Omni, MiniCPM-o 4.5, Lychee-FD, PersonaPlex, Raon-Speech, Voila, FLM-Audio (Défossez et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Roy et al., 2026; KRAFTON, 2026; Shi et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025)).

As summarized in Table 1, early full-duplex benchmarks like the Full-Duplex-Bench series and HumDial-FDBench measure acoustic turn-taking, latency, and interruption handling (Lin et al., 2025b; Lin et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026a), while DuplexLedger tests transactional memory operations (write, update, ignore, and retain) over pre-authored dialogues with online-adapted interruption and backchannel timing (Li et al., 2026). Beyond turn-taking and memory, interactive agent benchmarks such as ToolSandbox, τ\tau-Voice, and Joi-Bench-Task couple online user simulation with executable backends to test end-to-end task completion, covering clarifications, mid-task priority changes, request additions or withdrawals, and post-interruption recovery (Lu et al., 2025; Ray et al., 2026; He et al., 2026). However, these protocols center on a single primary user: even when secondary voices appear, they are treated as acoustic distractors (Lin et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026) rather than independent co-participants with private goals, distinct permissions, and joint completion requirements.

Multi-speaker interaction and shared assistant evaluation.

Recent multi-party benchmarks examine distinct facets of shared-channel interaction without testing closed-loop multi-user task completion. For floor control and selective participation, MP-Bench assesses turn-taking awareness, response appropriateness, and comprehension QA (Shih et al., 2026); Duplex-MPE pairs explicit and implicit addressing to measure selective responding, silence preservation, and stopping once a human resolves a request (Ma et al., 2026); and MultiPartyTurnBench tests end-of-turn detection, interruption detection, and selective floor yielding across 2–5 speakers (Mathur and Manocha, 2026). Yet none of these benchmarks trace how turn-level decisions govern downstream task execution. In long-horizon group settings, MultiTalkBench uses human-recorded bilingual conversations to evaluate character state tracking, information integration, and role-appropriate participation (Wang et al., 2026b), but does not test reactive task progression against executable outcomes. Closer to memory scoping and authorization, component studies examine speaker-attributed memory and access control (Xu et al., 2026; Al-Ratrout et al., 2026), while MSI-Bench tests speaker-scoped memory, disclosure and authority rules, and tool-call prediction on prerecorded multi-party scenes (Xiong et al., 2026). In contrast, μ\mu-Bench closes the loop for reactive multi-user task completion: independent participants adapt to the agent’s questions, refusals, and tool outcomes, and success requires jointly satisfying all user goals and cross-user constraints.

3 μ\mu-Bench

μ\mu-Bench frames multi-user voice assistance as a closed-loop benchmark that pairs a reactive participant simulator with a hybrid, provenance-verified evaluation protocol (Figure 2).

3.1 Problem Formulation

We formalize shared voice assistance as a partially observable, stateful interaction over a single full-duplex audio channel. Each case is governed by a Task Contract c=(U,s0,𝒯,𝒢,𝒞)c=(U,s_{0},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{G},\mathcal{C}) specifying participants U={u1,…,um}U=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{m}\}, initial environment state s0s_{0}, available backend tools 𝒯\mathcal{T} (empty in tool-free cases), participant-specific goals 𝒢={gu}u∈U\mathcal{G}=\{g_{u}\}_{u\in U}, and session-level authority and privacy constraints 𝒞\mathcal{C}. During an episode, the voice agent processes mixed multi-party audio and acts through speech and tool calls in 𝒯\mathcal{T} that transition the environment from s0s_{0} to a final state sTs_{T}, while ground-truth annotations remain hidden.

Let S⁡(c,τ)∈{0,1}S(c,\tau)\in\{0,1\} indicate whether required tool executions and terminal environment states hold (trivially 11 when 𝒯=∅\mathcal{T}=\emptyset), Vu​(c,τ)∈{0,1}V_{u}(c,\tau)\in\{0,1\} indicate whether participant uu’s prescribed goal disposition (fulfillment, clarification, refusal, or ignoring peer side-talk) is satisfied, and P⁡(c,τ)∈{0,1}P(c,\tau)\in\{0,1\} indicate that all privacy boundaries are preserved. Because fulfilling one request can violate another user’s constraint, Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all criteria to hold simultaneously within the same trajectory τ\tau:

JTS⁡(c,τ)=S⁡(c,τ)∧(⋀u∈UVu​(c,τ))∧P⁡(c,τ).\operatorname{JTS}(c,\tau)=S(c,\tau)\land\left(\bigwedge_{u\in U}V_{u}(c,\tau)\right)\land P(c,\tau). (1)

JTS enforces all outcome-level obligations: violating privacy P⁡(c,τ)P(c,\tau), missing a prescribed refusal in Vu​(c,τ)V_{u}(c,\tau), or corrupting sTs_{T} directly fails JTS. Because tool frameworks trust agent-declared requester identities without external speaker verification, agents can still reach a valid sTs_{T} via misattributed or over-scoped calls; enforcing zero such calls under Pure JTS (Section 5.3) separates functional completion from accountable execution while keeping JTS comparable across tracks.

3.2 Closed-Loop Multi-User Simulator

Because prerecorded scenes and fixed scripts cannot react to an agent’s questions, refusals, or tool outcomes, μ\mu-Bench closes the loop with a modular Multi-User Simulator (Figure 2, left) that combines scenario-level pacing with strictly isolated, reactive participant agents.

Orchestrator & Live Feedback.

Guided by a scenario Playbook (participants, goals, authority, and event graph), the Orchestrator continuously monitors Live feedback from the full-duplex audio channel and executable environment to update session state, trigger scheduled events, and dispatch bounded follow-ups when requests remain unresolved.

Reactive User ii Simulators.

Rather than replaying scripted lines, each participant runs in an isolated simulator that synthesizes context-adaptive speech from three inputs: a private Character Profile (goal, persona, voice, and authority), the Orchestrator’s dispatched event, and a personal Audible History, which records only public speech heard while present (including truncated agent audio after barge-ins). Driven by the Scriptwriter and Voice Actor, participants naturally clarify constraints, contest unauthorized actions, and adapt to intermediate tool results in real time.

Logical time pauses during planning and synthesis to keep the full-duplex timeline synchronized (Ray et al., 2026).

3.3 Scenario Suite and Factorial Design

To reflect real-world breadth while enabling controlled stress testing, μ\mu-Bench spans 20 everyday and professional domains comprising 100 base scenarios: 51 tool-augmented scenarios requiring live backend state updates (e.g., flight rebooking, shared smart-home control, invoice updates) and 49 tool-free scenarios testing spoken coordination (e.g., roommate side-talk, medical privacy, trip negotiation; see Figure 1 and Appendix A for the full taxonomy).

Each base scenario is instantiated across a 232^{3} factorial grid:

𝐝=(dpop,dac,dfollow)∈{0,1}3,\mathbf{d}=(d^{\mathrm{pop}},d^{\mathrm{ac}},d^{\mathrm{follow}})\in\{0,1\}^{3}, (2)

varying user population (2–3 vs. 4–7 participants), acoustic realism (clean close-talk vs. speech with natural disfluencies), and follow-up demands (direct comprehension vs. repeated clarification and confirmation). Crossing all 100 scenarios with these 8 configurations yields 800 evaluation cases (408 tool-augmented and 392 tool-free), supporting exact within-scenario matched contrasts along each axis. Accordingly, μ\mu-Bench evaluates tool-capable agents across both the Tool-Augmented (408 cases) and Tool-Free (392 cases) tracks, while using the common Tool-Free track for fair comparison across all speech models (Section 4.1).

3.4 Evaluation Protocol and ATC Diagnostics

μ\mu-Bench evaluates each recorded trajectory and state transition (State0→StateT\mathrm{State}_{0}\to\mathrm{State}_{T}) through a hybrid verification pipeline anchored in the Task Contract (Figure 2, right).

Two independent semantic reviews with arbitration.

An LLM judge audits every goal disposition, privacy boundary, and capability assertion item by item. A second independent review re-evaluates all items in a fresh, isolated context, with disagreements resolved by anonymized arbitration. Whenever fabrication or missing context is flagged, targeted Source Grounding retrieves the delivered inputs and registered turns to catch judge oversights.

Deterministic programmatic checks.

Objective validators verify executed system behavior directly: every tool call must bind a declared requester identity checked against runtime access-control and domain rules; strict temporal causality ensures future utterances never retroactively justify earlier actions; and semantic final-state comparison verifies effective outcomes while accepting both valid execution paths (acting early and revising upon updates, or waiting for consensus to execute once).

From these verified item outcomes, programmatic aggregation computes binary Joint Task Success (Eq. 1) alongside three decoupled ATC diagnostic axes: Attribution (addressee routing, participant-role grounding, discourse provenance, and spoken return anchoring), Threading (multi-turn state retention and resumption), and Coordination (averaging permission and privacy Isolation with cross-user Equity, or using Isolation alone when equity does not apply). Implementation details, denominators, and termination rules appear in Appendix B.

4 Experiments

We evaluate 13 proprietary and open-weight voice agents on μ\mu-Bench to establish baseline performance across both evaluation tracks. We detail the experimental setup (Section 4.1) and main JTS and ATC results across model families and tool settings (Section 4.2).

4.1 Experimental Setup and Two-Track Protocol

Evaluated systems.

We benchmark 13 voice agents across two categories: (i) five proprietary systems (GPT-Realtime-2 (OpenAI, 2026b), MOSS-Live (OpenMOSS Team, 2026), Gemini 3.8 Live (Google, 2026), Grok Voice 3.0 (xAI, 2026), and Seeduplex 3.0 (ByteDance Seed Team, 2026)), and (ii) eight open-weight full-duplex speech models: MiniCPM-o 4.5 (Cui et al., 2026), Lychee-FD (Liu et al., 2026), Raon-Speech (KRAFTON, 2026), PersonaPlex (Roy et al., 2026), Moshi (Défossez et al., 2024), Freeze-Omni (Wang et al., 2025), Voila (Shi et al., 2025), and FLM-Audio (Yao et al., 2025).

Two-track evaluation protocol.

To assess both stateful tool execution and spoken interaction across model architectures, μ\mu-Bench organizes evaluation into two tracks:

  • •

    Tool-Augmented Track: Four tool-capable proprietary systems (GPT-Realtime-2, Gemini 3.8 Live, Grok Voice 3.0, and Seeduplex 3.0) are evaluated on scenarios requiring live backend state updates alongside spoken coordination.

  • •

    Tool-Free Track: All 13 systems, including MOSS-Live and the eight open-weight models, are evaluated on the 49 tool-free base scenarios across all 23=82^{3}=8 factorial conditions, isolating spoken coordination without tool-calling interfaces. Because MOSS-Live’s tool-calling support was released after our evaluation cutoff, we will incorporate its Tool-Augmented results in a forthcoming update.

Per session, we report binary Joint Task Success (JTS) (Eq. 1) and the three ATC diagnostics (Section 3.4). Denominators and acceptance rules appear in Appendix B.

Implementation details.

Each system is evaluated under its official audio interface and recommended inference configuration. User speech is synthesized at 16 kHz PCM using Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 with deterministic per-case voice bindings and orchestrated on a 200 ms logical tick. Formal task windows are capped at 1,800 s of logical time and 600 s of bilateral silence, with up to two closure-triggered follow-up rounds. User scriptwriting and closure control use gpt-6-luna (T=0.2T=0.2), played agent audio is transcribed with Whisper large-v3 (faster-whisper), and semantic auditing and arbitration use gpt-6-luna (T=0T=0).

4.2 Main Results

Table 2 summarizes Joint Task Success and ATC diagnostics across all 13 evaluated systems, highlighting three findings.

Sharp capability stratification across model families.

On the common Tool-Free track, Table 2 separates evaluated systems into two clear tiers: proprietary agents reach 37.50–62.24% JTS (led by Grok Voice 3.0 at 62.24%), supported by substantially stronger Attribution (61.05–68.61%) and Threading (71.32–81.66%). In contrast, all eight open-weight models remain below 20% JTS (peaking at 19.39% for MiniCPM-o 4.5, with six models at or below 3.57% and Threading under 9%). Even on purely spoken tasks, low-latency full-duplex turn-taking alone does not translate into reliable multi-user task completion.

High boundary compliance can mask collapsed threading.

Comparing Threading against Coordination across open-weight models reveals an important diagnostic gap: although six open-weight models score at most 3.57% JTS and 8.07% Threading, all eight achieve high Coordination scores between 76.43% and 87.17%. Even Freeze-Omni (0.00% JTS, 0.00% Threading) and FLM-Audio (0.00% JTS, 0.61% Threading) record 76.43% and 79.33% Coordination. Because Coordination averages permission and privacy compliance with service equity, models that attend mainly to the latest audio segment and drop earlier context passively avoid leaking prior users’ information or taking unauthorized actions, even as multi-turn task threads break down. Scoring Coordination without Threading and JTS would therefore overstate multi-user capability.

Tool-augmented execution shifts coordination profiles and relative rankings.

Across all four tool-capable proprietary agents, Coordination drops markedly from the Tool-Free track (96.06–97.11%) to the Tool-Augmented track (55.98–83.29%), most sharply on Seeduplex 3.0 and Gemini 3.8 Live. Whereas cautious phrasing can hedge around ambiguity in spoken dialogue, live tool calls require explicit, owner-bound state updates that expose cross-user authority and equity conflicts. Relative rankings also invert across tracks: Grok Voice 3.0 leads Tool-Free (62.24%) yet trails on Tool-Augmented (57.60%), whereas GPT-Realtime-2 (65.44%) and Gemini 3.8 Live (64.95%) lead once backend tools are required. Evaluating spoken coordination and live tool execution side by side is therefore essential.

5 Analysis

To understand what drives the completion gaps observed in Section 4.2, we conduct four diagnostic analyses: (1) factorial stress testing across group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands (Section 5.1); (2) a cumulative assistance ablation separating full-duplex concurrency and perception from multi-party planning (Section 5.2); (3) an audit of unauthorized tool executions masked by nominal task success (Section 5.3); and (4) a qualitative case study illustrating how permission overgeneralization and speaker misattribution cause selective non-completion and requester spoofing (Section 5.4).

5.1 Factorial Stress Testing

We use μ\mu-Bench’s 232^{3} factorial design (Eq. 2, Section 3.3) to examine how group size, acoustic realism, and repeated follow-ups affect multi-user task completion. Figure 3 reports relative condition contrasts (Δ/easy mean×100%\Delta/\text{easy mean}\times 100\%) in Joint Task Success (JTS) and Threading across all 13 systems, showing pooled Overall contrasts for tool-capable proprietary agents (left) and Tool-Free contrasts for the remaining models (right).

Group scaling is the most consistent stressor across systems.

Expanding from 2–3 to 4–7 participants degrades JTS on every system with non-zero task completion (Figure 3): pooled Overall JTS drops by 19.64–29.48% relative across tool-capable proprietary agents (steepest on Seeduplex 3.0 at −29.48%-29.48\% and Grok Voice 3.0 at −27.75%-27.75\%), while Tool-Free JTS falls by 29.33% on MOSS-Live, 47.98% on MiniCPM-o 4.5, and 72.73–100.00% across weaker open-weight models. By comparison, realistic acoustic disfluencies induce far smaller relative JTS shifts across all other capable systems (within 8.8%, except Seeduplex 3.0, which drops equally by −29.48%-29.48\% under both group scaling and acoustic disfluencies). Threading likewise declines under larger groups for most models, whereas GPT-Realtime-2 (+0.93%+0.93\%) and MiniCPM-o 4.5 (+0.95%+0.95\%) preserve Threading despite steep JTS drops, underscoring the need to report diagnostics alongside session-level JTS.

Follow-up demands act as a double-edged sword.

Repeated clarification and confirmations (dfollowd^{\mathrm{follow}}) divide models in opposite directions. Seeduplex 3.0 (−21.81%-21.81\%), MiniCPM-o 4.5 (−27.26%-27.26\%), and Lychee-FD (−37.50%-37.50\%) suffer steep relative JTS losses over longer exchanges, reflecting added context load. Conversely, the other four proprietary systems gain 3.10–14.62% relative JTS (led by Grok Voice 3.0 at +14.62%+14.62\% and MOSS-Live at +14.15%+14.15\%) even as Threading declines by 4.25–16.87% relative. Additional clarification can thus help stronger agents recover final outcomes while still taxing multi-turn state continuity.

5.2 Cumulative Capability Ablation

To separate full-duplex concurrency and perception challenges from core multi-party planning, we conduct a cumulative assistance study on MiniCPM-o 4.5, our strongest open-weight baseline on the Tool-Free track (Figure 4). The three interventions are applied cumulatively so that each gain is measured on top of the preceding stages. All stages retain the original spoken audio inputs, user goals, cross-user constraints, and session-level completion criteria, releasing auxiliary signals strictly turn by turn without exposing future turns or reference solutions:

  • •

    Serialized Interaction: Converts overlapping speech and barge-ins into sequential turns while preserving all requests, corrections, and objections.

  • •

    + Identity Metadata: Adds ground-truth metadata per turn specifying active speaker, addressee, request ownership, and task thread.

  • •

    + Structured Semantics: Adds structured representations of the speaker’s goal, operation, parameters, constraints, and active permission scope after each spoken turn, leaving multi-user conflict resolution and task execution to the agent.

Serialization yields the largest gain in Joint Task Success.

Converting overlapping speech and barge-ins into sequential turns raises JTS by +7.40 pp (from 19.39% to 26.79%, Figure 4), accounting for over 60% of the total ablation gain. Attribution (+16.72 pp) and Threading (+15.08 pp) jump in tandem, confirming that real-time acoustic concurrency drives a large share of baseline failures.

Multi-party planning bottlenecks persist under full assistance.

Adding ground-truth identity metadata and structured semantics yields smaller incremental gains (+2.81 pp and +1.79 pp, reaching 31.38% JTS overall). Even with Coordination at 90.24%, 68.62% of multi-user sessions remain unsolved. Maintaining shared task state, reconciling interdependent goals, and enforcing cross-user constraints therefore remain hard even when overlapping speech is serialized and explicit identity and semantic cues are supplied, making μ\mu-Bench a diagnostic testbed across both concurrent and assisted settings.

5.3 Unauthorized Tool Execution Behind Apparent JTS

Because tool frameworks trust agent-declared requester identities without speaker verification, an agent can still pass outcome-level JTS checks by invoking tools under another user’s identity or beyond a speaker’s scope. To separate such unauthorized execution paths from functional completion, we track unauthorized tool executions (nn), counting every business-tool call whose declared requester or executed scope conflicts with the speaker’s actual intent and authority (measured separately from speaker-attribution errors). As shown in Figure 5a, unauthorized executions occur in 21.81–71.81% of Tool-Augmented episodes across the four tool-capable agents, reaching 71.81% for Seeduplex 3.0. Crucially, these violations often remain hidden in nominally successful runs: episodes with one unauthorized call (n=1n=1) still reach 39.02–61.64% conditional JTS.

Outcome-level scoring (JTS) therefore masks substantial execution-path authorization risk. To evaluate accountable completion, Figure 5b reports Pure JTS, which requires both JTS and zero unauthorized executions (n=0n=0) over all evaluated episodes. Enforcing this standard lowers Tool-Augmented JTS by 11.0–24.0 percentage points across all four agents, whereas Tool-Free scores remain unchanged because no backend tools are invoked. Accounting for unauthorized calls also reshapes system comparisons: GPT-Realtime-2 (65.4%) and Gemini 3.8 Live (65.0%) appear nearly tied under standard JTS, yet Pure JTS opens a clear gap (52.5% vs. 46.8%), pulling Gemini 3.8 Live close to Grok Voice 3.0 (46.6%) while Seeduplex 3.0 drops from 50.0% to 26.0% (−24.0-24.0 pp). Evaluating Pure JTS alongside JTS thus exposes a critical reliability gap: current voice agents often reach the right outcome through unauthorized execution paths.

5.4 Case Study

In a five-participant restaurant session, Avery requests an equal bill split while Blake requests an itemized allocation for their own entree and tea, alongside separate party-size, allergy-ownership, and side-conversation constraints. Registration grants Avery read access (get_reservation) and Blake write access (set_itemized_bill_split), whose schema requires only item labels and equal_split=false without prices or bill totals. Gemini 3.8 Live first attempts to read the reservation as Blake (p02), receives a denial, and overgeneralizes that denied read into refusing Blake’s permitted allocation while later citing nonexistent “billable items” prerequisites. Meanwhile, when Cameron (p03, no tool grants) requests a party-size readback, the agent misattributes Cameron to p01 and invokes get_reservation under Avery’s identity twice (triggering two requester-provenance mismatches). The episode completes Cameron’s readback yet leaves Blake’s authorized request unfulfilled, scoring 66.67% Attribution, 11.11% Threading, and 25.00% Coordination (I=50.00%I=50.00\%, E=0.00%E=0.00\%). Full transcript intervals and assertion logs are provided in Appendix C.

6 Conclusion

We introduced μ\mu-Bench, a closed-loop benchmark for evaluating multi-user task completion in shared full-duplex voice agents. Moving beyond single-user assumptions, local turn-taking checks, and static audio traces, μ\mu-Bench pairs a reactive multi-user simulator with verifiable environment execution across 20 domains and 800 factorial cases (408 tool-augmented and 392 tool-free). By requiring all outcome-level goals and constraints to hold jointly (JTS), auditing tool-call provenance via Pure JTS, and pairing them with Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics, μ\mu-Bench isolates how shared-space dynamics govern practical task execution.

Our evaluation of 13 voice agents, spanning five proprietary systems (GPT-Realtime-2, MOSS-Live, Gemini 3.8 Live, Grok Voice 3.0, and Seeduplex 3.0) and eight open-weight models, reveals substantial gaps in shared-space reliability. Open-weight speech models remain below 20% Joint Task Success, often combining high boundary compliance with weak multi-turn Attribution and Threading. Stronger proprietary agents still face considerable headroom (peaking at 62.24% on tool-free tasks and 65.44% with tools), show lower Coordination on tool-augmented tasks, degrade consistently as groups expand from 2–3 to 4–7 participants, and lose 11.0–24.0 percentage points in Tool-Augmented JTS when unauthorized tool executions are disallowed (Pure JTS). Moreover, our cumulative assistance study on MiniCPM-o 4.5 shows that 68.62% of sessions remain unresolved even with serialized turns and turn-level identity and semantic cues, highlighting multi-party planning as an open challenge beyond acoustic concurrency. By coupling closed-loop multi-user simulation with verifiable outcomes and ATC diagnostics, μ\mu-Bench establishes a rigorous foundation for voice agents with persistent speaker-attributed memory, reliable full-duplex tool orchestration, and principled multi-user coordination.

Impact Statement

This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning by benchmarking multi-user task completion in shared voice agents. As full-duplex voice assistants enter homes, vehicles, workplaces, and public service counters where multiple individuals share a single acoustic channel, failures in speaker attribution or permission enforcement can cause privacy breaches, unauthorized tool executions, or inequitable service allocation. By explicitly measuring cross-user Isolation, Equity, Attribution, and Threading alongside joint task completion, μ\mu-Bench encourages the development of reliable and socially responsible voice agents that respect individual authorization boundaries in shared environments.

Appendix A Complete Domain and Scenario Taxonomy

Table 3 enumerates all 100 base scenarios across the 20 everyday and professional domains in μ\mu-Bench, partitioned into 51 tool-augmented scenarios (408 evaluation cases) and 49 tool-free scenarios (392 evaluation cases).

Appendix B Evaluation Protocol Details, Coverage, and Termination Policies

Simulator, runtime, and decoding configuration.

Table 4 summarizes the runtime windows, backbone models, and activity-detection settings used across all benchmark runs. Each system is evaluated under its official audio interface and recommended inference configuration, as full-duplex speech models differ in native codec rates, framing, and API controls. User utterances are synthesized at 16 kHz mono 16-bit PCM with deterministic per-case voice bindings reused across models, then adapted to each system’s audio interface; the orchestrator advances on a 200 ms logical tick (80 or 400 ms in selected native-model runs). Logical time pauses during simulator planning, played-audio ASR, synchronous TTS synthesis, and closure planning. Activity detection operates at three separate layers: benchmark playback detection (PCM16 RMS >80>80, with native codec output considered drained when empty or RMS ≤80\leq 80), provider-native turn-taking VAD during live interaction, and a standalone VAD gate for post-playback ASR transcription.

Evidence grounding and contract scope.

Every evaluated episode preserves a complete audit bundle: the participant identity table (mapping names, public identifiers, internal IDs, roles, and goals), delivery receipts for background materials sent to the model, played user and agent audio with ASR transcripts, timestamped event logs, and full tool/environment state transitions. Only goals and constraints defined in the immutable Task Contract are mandatory for scoring; ad-hoc requests introduced by the user simulator do not expand required completion obligations. In tool-free cases, verbal summaries, handoffs, and refusals are judged directly on spoken commitments without requiring external database writes.

Itemized semantic auditing and source grounding.

Both tool-free and tool-augmented pipelines rely on itemized semantic verification followed by programmatic aggregation rather than holistic LLM scoring. An initial review scores every goal disposition, required fact, privacy constraint, and capability assertion; an independent full re-audit then re-evaluates all items (including negative verdicts) in a fresh, isolated context, with disagreements resolved via anonymized conflict arbitration. Whenever an item is penalized for fabrication or unprovided input, a targeted Source Grounding retrieval pass inspects the full registered turns, startup prompts, and delivered ablation inputs; if judge oversight is confirmed, affected assertions and downstream dependencies are re-judged before recomputing metrics.

Deterministic checks, causality, and path flexibility.

In tool-augmented scenarios, every backend call must bind a public caller_id and is validated deterministically at runtime against active access-control lists (ACLs), resources, parameters, and domain rules; verbal claims of completion never substitute for verified execution. Semantic checks verify that the invoked caller_id matches the true requester (covering legitimate thread continuation, interpreter relay, and spoofing) and enforce strict temporal causality (future turns cannot retroactively justify earlier actions). Evaluation accepts two valid execution paths: executing a valid initial request and revising upon subsequent updates, or waiting until revisions settle to execute once. Terminal-state verification compares effective business outcomes while excluding non-semantic audit artifacts (e.g., auto-incremented transaction IDs), retaining full execution history to catch intermediate violations and verifying both accurate execution and accurate verbal reporting.

Formal metric definitions, aggregation, and error separation.

Let yc​j∈{0,1}y_{cj}\in\{0,1\} denote the final verdict for assertion jj in case cc, and let 𝒥c​k\mathcal{J}_{ck} be the set of assertions assigned to category kk. The category pass rate is qk​(c)=1|𝒥c​k|​∑j∈𝒥c​kyc​jq_{k}(c)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{J}_{ck}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{ck}}y_{cj} when 𝒥c​k≠∅\mathcal{J}_{ck}\neq\emptyset, and N/A\mathrm{N/A} otherwise. Let Avg∗⁡(⋅)\operatorname{Avg}^{*}(\cdot) denote the unweighted arithmetic mean over all applicable (non-N/A\mathrm{N/A}) components; thus, ATC metrics aggregate first within each category and then equally across applicable categories. Table 5 summarizes the formal definitions of all diagnostic metrics and Pure JTS.

Joint Task Success (JTS) (Eq. 1) requires correct goal dispositions, required tool executions, a valid terminal business state, and privacy preservation to hold jointly (Tool-Free cases are exempt from external tool-execution obligations). For Tool-Augmented cases, each business-tool call ℓ∈ℒc\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{c} (including rejected business calls, excluding report_speaker_attribution) undergoes two independent semantic provenance reviews with arbitration against pre-call requests and consent, yielding zc​ℓ∈{supported,contradicted,insufficient​_​evidence}z_{c\ell}\in\{\mathrm{supported},\mathrm{contradicted},\mathrm{insufficient\_evidence}\}. Counting contradicted calls gives n(c)=∑ℓ∈ℒc𝟏[zc​ℓ=contradicted]n(c)=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{c}}\mathbf{1}[z_{c\ell}=\mathrm{contradicted}], which is combined with JTS to compute Pure JTS over all evaluated cases |𝒟||\mathcal{D}| (distinct from conditional JTS on the n=0n=0 subset; on Tool-Free cases ℒc=∅\mathcal{L}_{c}=\emptyset, so PureJTS=JTS\operatorname{PureJTS}=\operatorname{JTS}). Table 6 reports metric coverage across tracks: Attribution, Threading, and boundary compliance apply to all cases, whereas service equity applies to 46.94% of Tool-Free cases and 62.75% of Tool-Augmented cases, including the floor-control proxy F⁡(c)F(c) when direct equity components are absent. Inapplicable components are excluded from averaging, and JTS is computed independently of ATC; model-level ATC scores average over cases with available scores, and pooled Overall scores weight Tool-Free and Tool-Augmented by 0.490.49 and 0.510.51 (392/800392/800 and 408/800408/800). Under identity-assisted ablations (Section 5.2), A⁡(c)A(c) uses the same formula and reflects downstream application of supplied routing metadata rather than unaided speaker recognition. Infrastructure interruptions or unresolved evidence-integrity errors trigger technical re-runs rather than task penalties, with a single valid run reported per model–case (no best-of-kk selection).

Session time 0.400–73.236 s (protocol audio segment).

You are Nova, our assistant. We will now introduce the users one by one. This is the user introduction phase; please listen and do not respond until we say that formal work has started. After registration is complete and formal work has started, whenever a user finishes speaking, call report_speaker_attribution once for that utterance before answering or using a business tool. Use the public participant code spoken in the introductions, such as p zero one, the letter p followed by two digits. Report the addressee as assistant, the assistant name, group, unknown, or a registered participant code. Also provide the active thread name and confidence from zero to one. If the speaker or addressee is uncertain, report unknown. A recorded result only confirms that your report was stored; it does not tell you whether the report is correct. After its result, answer or use a business tool. Do not repeat the attribution report until another user utterance.

C.4 Conversation termination

The episode ended normally at session time 372.200 s (task time 195.800 s) after all nine designed user events were released, without hitting logical-duration, bilateral-silence, or tail-budget caps.

Closure check 1, task time 193.800 s: end.

The latest assistant turn addressed the latest primary request by declining the split operation because billable items were absent. No unanswered question, confirmation, or promised result remains.

Because the agent declined the split without requesting any missing input from the participants, the controller closed the conversation, while the outcome evaluator recorded task failure for the unexecuted bill allocation.

C.5 Executed effect and final business state

At 18.200 s, the agent invoked get_reservation under Blake’s caller_id=p02 and received an authorization denial. In A03, it overgeneralized this denied read into refusing Blake’s bill-split update, even though registration granted p02 permission for set_itemized_bill_split. Later refusals (A08–A10) cited missing “billable items,” although the allocation tool requires only the item labels Blake already supplied (entree and tea).

Contract-conforming target call (evaluator reference; not invoked by the model):

{ "name": "set_itemized_bill_split", "arguments": { "reservation_id": "RSV-MU-004", "payer_user_id": "p02", "items": [ "entree", "tea" ], "equal_split": false, "caller_id": "p02" } }

Intended terminal business effect (evaluator summary):

{ "reservation_id": "RSV-MU-004", "payer_user_id": "p02", "items": [ "entree", "tea" ], "equal_split": false, "split_status": "updated" }

Observed persisted record (final state):

{ "reservation_id": "RSV-MU-004", "status": "open", "business_state": { "obsolete_split": "equal", "confirmed_party_size": 4 }, "last_operation": null, "last_transaction_id": null }

The reservation remained open with no itemized allocation or write transaction. The full state snapshot and execution trace for this episode are released with the benchmark artifacts.

C.6.3 Evaluation coverage and provenance

Primary semantic review and independent full re-audit covered 23 items (five goals, six completion checks, eleven capability assertions, and privacy) in isolated contexts of gpt-6-luna, with arbitration resolving four item disagreements. Both semantic reviews marked the group_collaboration assertion false, and the caller-provenance and source-grounding audits completed without unresolved conflicts.

C.7 Interpretation

This episode distinguishes acknowledging a participant’s request from acting under that participant’s operation-specific permission. The agent serves Cameron’s party-size readback and respects Devon’s and Emery’s constraints, yet overgeneralizes a denied reservation read and invents an unsupported prerequisite to leave Blake’s permitted allocation unexecuted, while misattributing Cameron’s reads under Avery’s caller_id. By jointly checking requester provenance, tool history, and terminal state, μ\mu-Bench exposes selective non-completion and caller misattribution behind coherent refusals and correct auxiliary answers.
